I've been farming this land for three decades. My farm is small — 4.1 mu — but my family depends on it for staple food, and the off-farm income from my kids lets me invest a bit more carefully rather than cutting every corner. I'm not running after maximum yield at any cost. I've watched the water table in Quzhou drop for twenty years. I have a university education and I've read the research. I know I need to be smarter about water and fertilizer than older farmers were.

For **winter wheat**, I'll plant in early October after rotary-tilling the maize stubble back into the soil. I'll use Kenong 199 or a similarly adapted improved variety — not the cheapest seed, but proven in this county. I'll apply base fertilizer (phosphorus and potassium all at once, plus a third of my nitrogen), then topdress nitrogen at jointing stage. I'll irrigate at sowing, jointing, and heading — three times. I used to do four, but the research out of China Agricultural University convinced me the third irrigation at grain fill isn't worth the groundwater draw in most years. Three fungicide/herbicide/insecticide passes are standard; I won't skip any of those.

For **summer maize**, I'll direct-seed into the wheat stubble right after June harvest — no tillage. I'll use Xianyu 335 hybrid seed. Summer maize in Hebei catches the July–August monsoon, so I'll only irrigate if there's drought stress at emergence or tasseling — planning for two irrigations but ready to skip one if rains come. I'll apply nitrogen in two splits: base plus a top-dress at the 10-leaf stage.

Both crops share the same 4.0 mu of cultivated area (0.1 mu is path and well infrastructure).
